Determine whether training can improve low-rank compressibility while preserving model quality.

sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

passages.text: However, we argue that this trade-off is not fundamental. Spectral regularization may be most valuable early, when it can shape the optimization trajectory, yet become a liability if maintained as the weights adapt to the task. The two effects need not be accepted together: we can use the constraint to shape the spectrum, then release it before it restricts the final solution. This motivates a minimal method ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After): During an initial phase, ORCA applies a soft orthogonality penalty, R orth ​ ( 𝐖 ) = 1 4 ​ ‖ 𝐖𝐖 ⊤ − 𝐈 ‖ F 2 R_{\mathrm{orth}}(\mathbf{W})=\frac{1}{4}\|\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\top}-\mathbf{I}\|_{F}^{2} . Then directly removes it at a single switch point. Training thereafter follows the standard optimizer update, with no gradual decay or further changes. This design lets early regularization influence the optimization path without prescribing the spectrum throughout training. In our experiments, this simple release is followed by faster loss reduction and a lower final validation loss than Muon. Figure 1.1: LLaMA 130M training dynamics. Effective rank is measured on a middle-layer V V projection; the dashed line marks regularization release. Figure 1.1 illustrates the transition. While the penalty is active, the effective rank of the weight matrix rises sharply above Muon’s, although ORCA initially has a higher validation loss. After release, the rank falls from its peak but remains above Muon’s, while validation loss decreases rapidly, crosses the Muon curve. The result is consistent with early spectral shaping leaving a useful effect on the subsequent trajectory, even after the explicit penalty is gone. Controlled interventions in Section 5 further investigates into this connection.

We evaluate ORCA on LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained MoE models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, including 100B-token training runs. ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon across these settings. In most experiments, the reduction is 0.02–0.04, comparable to or greater than Muon’s gain over Adam. To put this loss reduction in perspective, on LLaMA 1.3B, ORCA achieving the 0.024 lower validation loss reaches Muon’s 100k-step loss in just 60k steps. Further, downstream evaluations, alternative early spectral interventions, multi-seed runs, and ablations of method parameters and intervention timing further support these gains. Together, these results show that early spectral shaping followed by constraint relaxation can improve training efficiency and final performance across architectures without substantial changes to the optimizer. To summarize the contributions of the paper: (1) We illustrate a trade-off in spectral control through a simplified model and empirical observations: favorable spectra can accelerate optimization but persistent constraints may harm the attainable solution quality. (2) We introduce ORCA, a minimal shape-then-release optimizer that leverages early orthogonal regularization to improve optimization trajectories while allowing unconstrained adaptation in later training. (3) We demonstrate ORCA’s effectiveness across diverse LLM architectures and scales, achieving faster convergence and lower loss than existing optimizers. Through extensive controlled experiments, we further validate the mechanism that early effective-rank shaping drives the observed improvements.

The advantage of ORCA holds over a wide range of learning rates: at every learning rate evaluated for both methods, ORCA reaches a lower final validation loss than Muon, and at all evaluated configurations between 10 − 3 10^{-3} and 5 × 10 − 3 5\times 10^{-3} it is even better than fully tuned Muon. The independent searches select 1.3 × 10 − 3 1.3\times 10^{-3} , 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} , 10 − 3 10^{-3} , and 2 × 10 − 3 2\times 10^{-3} for Adam, Muon, Pion, and ORCA, with final validation losses of 2.8824 2.8824 , 2.8460 2.8460 , 2.9790 2.9790 , and 2.8106 2.8106 , respectively; ORCA thus lowers the loss by a further 0.0354 0.0354 relative to the best Muon and stays within 0.002 0.002 of its own optimum across 1.6 × 10 − 3 1.6\times 10^{-3} to 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} , showing that the improvement does not rely on a narrow learning-rate choice. LLama Pretraining Tasks. We compare ORCA against Adam and Muon on LLaMA 350M and 1.3B, training each model for 100B tokens. As shown in Figure 4.1 , Muon outperforms Adam at both scales, while ORCA further lowers the validation loss. Compared with Muon, ORCA reduces the final loss by 0.0194 0.0194 at 350M and 0.0244 0.0244 at 1.3B, with consistent gains at both scales. Further, a four-seed robustness result for the 130M, 50k-step setting is reported in Appendix C . We also evaluate the final ORCA and Muon LLaMA 1.3B checkpoints from Figure 4.1 on five downstream tasks ( Clark et al., 2018 ; Zellers et al., 2019 ; Sakaguchi et al., 2021 ; Bisk et al., 2020 ) . As shown in Table 4.1 , ORCA outperforms Muon on all five tasks. This suggests that the lower pre-training loss of ORCA also leads to better downstream performance.

We also evaluate how the optimization performance translates into token efficiency by measuring the training required to reach a common target loss. We continued ORCA from its original 51k-step checkpoint, starting the final decay early, and reached a validation loss of 2.318 at approximately 60k steps. The standard Muon run, using its original 100k-step settings, reached the same loss at 100k steps ( Figure 2(a) ). Therefore, ORCA used 40% fewer tokens to reach this target, a 1.66× token-efficiency gain. To save compute, we reused the checkpoint without retuning ORCA for the shorter run: its original 25k-step shaping stage accounts for 41.7% of the 60k-step budget rather than the tuned default of 25%. Qwen3 Pretraining Tasks. We compare Adam, Muon, and ORCA on Qwen3-style architecture. Within each model scale, all methods share the same common hyperparameters. The Qwen3 0.6B curves cover 50k optimizer steps (about 105B tokens), and the Qwen3 160M curves cover 25k optimizer steps (about 26B tokens). In both Qwen settings, both sets of loss curves show the same ordering: ORCA may fall temporarily behind Muon early in training, then crosses over and holds the advantage at the end of the observed interval. The validation-loss improvement of ORCA is therefore not confined to LLaMA, but also reproduces on the Qwen3 architecture. Larger Scale Fine-grained MoE Pretrining. We observed router perturbations under a fixed global release point, so we release the orthogonal constraint layerwise: at 20 % 20\% of training in the first layer and at 60 % 60\% in the last layer, with release times linearly interpolated across layers. We use top- 4 4 routing with 64 64 experts in the MoE 0.8 0.8 B model ( 0.24 0.24 B active parameters) and 64 64 experts in the MoE 8 8 B model ( 1 1 B active parameters) ( Dai et al., 2024 ) . Due to computational budget constraints, we focus our comparison on Muon and ORCA. ORCA achieves the lowest final loss at both 25 25 B and 50 50 B tokens for the 0.8 0.8 B model, showing that its gain persists as the token budget increases. The 8 8 B experiment extends this result to a larger model trained on 100 100 B tokens, where ORCA also finishes below Muon ( Figure 4.4 ). Across these MoE experiments, ORCA reduces final validation loss by 0.020 0.020 – 0.025 0.025 relative to Muon.

Early orthogonal shaping also benefits other base optimizers. We apply the same soft orthogonal shaping step ( 3.3 ) to Adam and SOAP on LLaMA 130M ( Vyas et al., 2025 ) . Shaping is active only during the first 25 % 25\% of training; the base optimizer then continues alone. For both optimizers, shaping temporarily raises validation loss while active, but the shaped runs overtake their baselines after its removal and finish lower. At 50k steps, it reduces Adam’s loss from 2.8824 2.8824 to 2.8435 2.8435 and SOAP’s from 2.8640 2.8640 to 2.8271 2.8271 , gains of 0.0389 0.0389 and 0.0369 0.0369 , respectively. These results show that the benefits of early orthogonal shaping extend beyond Muon to other base optimizers. matches.title: Lightweight and Versatile Learned Optimization by Recombination of Gradient History
matches.abstract_excerpt: This paper presents a lightweight and versatile learned optimizer that dynamically recombines gradient history, represented as averages over disjoint time spans. The optimizer reduces the prediction space to one scalar coefficient per gradient average, shared by multiple parameters. Progressively averaging older gradients minimizes memory cost of long history, while keeping their contributions independently accessible. A 37k-parameter network trained in 0.87 GPU-hours generalizes zero-shot to unseen tasks, lowering validation loss by 9.1% and 0.4% on BERT-Tiny and GPT-Tiny, and improving test accuracy over Adam by 3.5 %p on a Vision Transformer and by 2.7 %p on average across nine graph models, with FLOPs overhead as low as 0.3%.

passages.text: BRAIn Lab Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights Dmitrii Andriianov 1 , Andrey Veprikov 1,2 , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1,3 1 Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab) 2 SB AI Lab 3 Innopolis University Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. Under fixed-horizon training with 60 % 60\% label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization by up to 17.8 17.8 points on MNIST and 4.6 4.6 points across four BERT-base tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SpectralWD .

To make the regularizer matrix-aware, we begin with the proximal interpretation of decoupled weight decay. To first order, its update is a proximal gradient step for the squared Frobenius penalty [ Parikh and Boyd, 2014 ; Zhuang et al., 2022 ] . We replace this penalty with the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank whose proximal operator soft-thresholds singular values [ Recht et al., 2010 ; Cai et al., 2010 ] . This construction is the matrix analogue of replacing ridge shrinkage with coefficient selection by the lasso [ Hoerl and Kennard, 1970 ; Tibshirani, 1996 ] . Given the loss-only optimizer direction Δ \Delta , let Z = W ( k ) − η ​ Δ = U Z ​ Σ Z ​ V Z ⊤ Z=W^{(k)}-\eta\Delta=U_{Z}\Sigma_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top} . Spectral weight decay applies the post-step correction W ( k + 1 ) = Z − η ​ λ ​ U Z ​ V Z ⊤ , W^{(k+1)}=Z-\eta\lambda U_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top}, (1) where η \eta is the learning rate and λ \lambda the regularization coefficient. This correction acts additively in the singular basis of Z Z , whereas conventional weight decay scales the spectrum uniformly. SLORR-Nuc also approximates the nuclear-norm polar factor [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Its decoupled extension would use the pre-step correction Z − η ​ λ ​ U W ​ V W ⊤ Z-\eta\lambda U_{W}V_{W}^{\top} for W ( k ) = U W ​ Σ W ​ V W ⊤ W^{(k)}=U_{W}\Sigma_{W}V_{W}^{\top} , rather than ( 1 ).

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. Beyond compression, we test whether the same low-rank bias limits memorization under label noise. We evaluate spectral weight decay in LLaMA [ Touvron et al., 2023 ] pretraining, post-training compression, and fixed-horizon noisy-label classification. Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and a 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. At 60 % 60\% label noise, mean clean-test accuracy gains over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization reach 17.78 17.78 points on MNIST and 4.59 4.59 points on four BERT-base tasks.

inspect:2610.10965.question: On CIFAR-10 and NanoGPT, how do Spectrally Targeted Muon variants compare with Muon and SGD in validation loss or speed, effective rank, and optimizer compute overhead? Were training budgets and hyperparameters matched?

passages.text: The Muon optimizer orthogonalizes each update matrix, setting all of its singular values to one, and has proven highly effective for training large language models. It remains unclear, however, whether this success comes from amplifying small singular directions that gradient descent neglects or from suppressing large, degenerate directions that disrupt training. We introduce Spectrally Targeted Muon, which orthogonalizes only the singular values above or below a threshold τ \tau , so that varying τ \tau interpolates between normalized SGD and Muon. It isolates the relevant singular subspaces with projections computed by Newton-Schulz iteration on a shifted Gram matrix, so no SVD is needed. We evaluate these variants on the CIFAR-10 and NanoGPT speedruns, tracking the effective rank of gradient, update, and weight matrices and a new metric, the alignment of updates with the tangent space of the weight matrix’s isospectral manifold. We find three things. First, the small singular values of the momentum are not noise. Orthogonalizing everything except the few largest singular values of each matrix nearly matches Muon while touching only a small fraction of the momentum, whereas orthogonalizing only the top falls well short even though it holds almost all of it. On language models every momentum singular value is far below one, so targeted orthogonalization can only amplify, and Muon wins by making directions that are too small to train on at their raw scale trainable. Second, shrinking the largest singular values is what keeps the parameter spectrum flat; this is cheap, and it is not what drives the loss. Third, AdamW differs from Muon mainly in how slowly it builds structure, which explains its slower start and why warmup helps AdamW but only hurts Muon.

We train a six-layer convolutional neural network on the CIFAR-10 dataset, building off of Keller Jordan’s original speedrun using Muon ( Jordan, 2024 ) . We chose this approach because the speedrun ensures exhaustively tuned learning rates and architectures, making it less likely that our results are artifacts of hyperparameters. This dataset includes 50,000 training images divided into 10 classes, along with 10,000 images for validation ( Krizhevsky, 2009 ) . Figure 1: Mean evaluation accuracy across 20 trials for each variant, with error bars representing ± \pm 2 standard deviations away from the mean. Validation accuracy was used as the primary metric for model performance. Learning rates were held constant across all optimizers, including SGD, and equal Nesterov momentum was applied. Instead of random flips for augmentation, all data is flipped every epoch, which leads to faster training. Our standard Muon run was therefore nearly identical to the speedrun implementation, aside from a batch size of 500 rather than 2000 due to GPU limitations. Therefore, we achieved an accuracy of 93.6% as opposed to the 94% in Jordan’s paper. This aligns with existing work arguing that Muon takes particular advantage of large batch sizes in much larger models ( Shah et al., 2025 ) .

Figure 4: Effective rank of the gradient (a) and update (b), averaged over all matrices, and of the value (c), attention-output (d) and MLP (e) parameters, averaged over layers (seed 0). Dashed lines are the warmup variants, the dotted line in (a) marks the start of the learning rate cooldown, and the legend in (b) applies to all panels. We use the effective rank of the gradient and update matrix to help explain our optimizer performances. Since the gradient depends only on the surrounding loss landscape and not the optimizer, it tells us which optimizers enter parts of the loss landscape where many directions are available. This happens quickly for Muon and the targeted variants, while AdamW takes a few hundred steps to get there. During learning rate cooldown, this effective rank grows for every optimizer, because the leading singular values of the gradient shrink while its bulk stays put. In the river-valley picture of Wen et al. (2024) , the component of the gradient along the sharp valley walls dies with the learning rate while the component along the flat floor remains. Gradient rank thus tells us where the iterate sits in the valley, bouncing between the walls or settled on the floor. Meanwhile, the effective rank of the update shows the difference between the different types of targeting, with bottom targeting creating an update shaped like Muon’s, while top targeting creates an even lower rank update than AdamW. (a) Tangent alignment (b) Spectrum-changing update by singular direction (c) Final loss vs. parameter rank

Figure 5: How much of the update changes the spectrum, and where. (a) Log-barrier of the isospectral tangent fraction, averaged over matrices; the grey dotted line is the value for a random rotation, the orange dotted line marks the start of the learning rate cooldown, and dashed lines are the warmup variants. (b) Share of the spectrum-changing part of the update at each singular direction of the parameter, ranked by singular value, averaged over matrices and steps 100–1500; the dotted line is uniform. (c) Final validation loss against final parameter effective rank, including the learning rate controls; the bottom-targeted runs at τ ≤ 4 × 10 − 4 \tau\leq 4\times 10^{-4} leave their MLP output matrices barely trained. Next, we examined the parameter effective ranks across different types of Transformer parameters in Figure 4 (c)–(e). We were able to observe the same results as Wang et al. (2025) , who found that AdamW heavily reduces the effective rank of parameters, unlike Muon, giving Muon a richer associative memory and better performance on tail classes. However, top targeted variants fall the most, and their zero-initialized output projections never gain much rank at all. This implies that the rich learning is a direct consequence of participation by the small singular values.

The parameter effective rank depends on the part of the update that changes the spectrum, meaning the part aligned with the parameter’s own singular basis, and how concentrated it is in the leading directions of this basis. Figure 5 (b) shows this directly: the top targeted and AdamW curves peak at the leading directions, while Muon and the bottom arm stay near uniform. Intuitively, an update that keeps pushing along the leading singular directions of a matrix reinforces what is already there, while a full-spectrum update mostly rotates the basis and leaves the spectrum unchanged. Figure 5 (c) plots these against the final loss. Figure 5 (a) shows the same thing with the isospectral tangent metric of Section 3.3 . Every optimizer puts more of its update into the parameter’s own basis than a random update would, and tangent alignment rises for every optimizer over training, fastest during the cooldown. Among the targeted variants of Muon, the bottom targeted versions show higher alignment than Muon, while the top targeted versions show lower alignment. This is reversed compared to the CIFAR experiments, but it reveals the same underlying phenomenon. In the NanoGPT domain, the targeted region has its magnitude raised, while the remaining regions are relatively suppressed. Therefore, it is simply the top few directions of the gradient which lie within the existing basis of the parameter, and the more you shrink them in the update, the less poorly conditioned the parameter matrices become. Note that structure and performance don’t move together: AdamW collapses rank and still performs well, the bottom targeted variants keep Muon’s rank without matching its loss, and full-spectrum updates keep the spectrum flat for free. This suggests that keeping the spectrum flat is

passages.text: Recent progress of foundation models with deep neural networks, such as large vision and large language models, has been remarkable [ 39 , 17 , 10 , 61 , 2 ] . When transferring these pre-trained models to a specific downstream task, one popular technique is full fine-tuning that updates all the model parameters. However, full fine-tuning of large foundation models is impractical due to their large number of parameters, requiring high computational and storage costs for each task-specific model. To address this issue, parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques have become a promising alternative to full fine-tuning [ 25 , 44 , 21 , 22 , 18 ] . Among these techniques, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the de facto standard thanks to its simplicity and effectiveness [ 21 ] . Let W 0 , W ∈ ℝ m × n W_{0},W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} denote the weight matrices of a layer in the pre-trained and fine-tuned models, respectively. In LoRA, the weight update of full fine-tuning Δ ​ W ∈ ℝ m × n \Delta W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} from W 0 W_{0} to W W is approximated by low-rank matrix factorization 1 1 1 We here omit the scaling B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} by s ∈ ℝ s\in\mathbb{R} for simplicity as it can be merged into B B and A A [ 24 ] . as follows: W = W 0 + Δ ​ W ≈ W 0 + B ​ A ⊤ , \displaystyle W=W_{0}+\Delta W\approx W_{0}+BA^{\top}, (2) where B ∈ ℝ m × r B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r} and A ∈ ℝ n × r A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} are trainable factors. Let ℒ : ℝ m × n → ℝ \mathcal{L}:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} denote the loss function for a downstream task. Then, LoRA is formulated as min ( B , A ) ∈ 𝒳 ⁡ ℒ ⁡ ( W 0 + B ​ A ⊤ ) , \min_{(B,A)\in\mathcal{X}}\mathcal{L}\left(W_{0}+BA^{\top}\right), (3)

LoRA was initially formulated by Hu et al. [21] and achieves comparable full fine-tuning performance despite having very few trainable parameters. These compact representations support both model updates and efficient policy synchronization. To prevent overly large updates from disrupting learning, we complement gradient compression with predicted-KL step control, which estimates policy changes before applying each update and adjusts its magnitude accordingly. With all techniques combined, LoGRA reduces average training memory usage by up to 45.7% across reasoning tasks without compromising performance. It also enables stable training of a 27B-parameter model for over 1,100 steps on a single eight-GPU node, where dense Adam runs out of memory, making previously memory-infeasible RL training practical. Code is available in the Molt library . \abscontent

Figure 1: Lower training memory across model scales. Colors denote model sizes; hatching distinguishes Dense Adam from LoGRA. Dark bars show average memory and pale extensions reach peak memory (Table 1 ); labels report average / peak in GiB per training GPU. Arrows show average-memory savings over Dense Adam. The broken axis omits 34–48 GiB. The 27B Dense Adam bar marks OOM at GPU capacity, not a measured value. Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a key driver of advances in LLM, enabling models to improve through feedback on their own generated responses ( Sheng et al., 2024 ; , 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . However, its substantial memory requirements remain a major barrier to broader adoption. This challenge extends well beyond storing model parameters, as gradients and optimizer states can consume several times more memory than the weights themselves. For example, the BF16 weights of a 7B-parameter Qwen model ( Bai et al., 2023 ) require approximately 14 GB, while Adam’s ( Kingma and Ba, 2014 ) two FP32 moment buffers add another 56 GB, even before accounting for gradients and activations. Consequently, hardware capable of running a model may still be insufficient to improve it through RL. Reducing this memory overhead is therefore critical to making RL post-training accessible to the broader research community.

To overcome this bottleneck, existing approaches span both system-level optimizations and memory-efficient training algorithms. At the system level, FSDP ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) shards training states across GPUs, gradient checkpointing ( Chen et al., 2016 ) reduces activation storage through recomputation, and CPU offloading moves selected training states to host memory ( Rajbhandari et al., 2020 ) . Parameter-efficient methods reduce the number of parameters that require gradients and optimizer states: LoRA ( Hu et al., 2021 ) , for example, freezes pretrained weights and learns small low-rank adapters. Gradient compression offers another route ( Zhao et al., 2024 ; Su et al., 2025 ; Hao et al., 2024 ) : they keep the original weight matrices trainable while using compact representations of gradients and optimizer states, thereby reducing training memory while still enabling effective updates to the full model.

We primarily compare LoGRA with dense-gradient training on DAPO-Math-7.5K. We evaluate on MATH-500 every five updates for the 1.5B and 7B models and every ten updates for the 27B model. Each batch contains 128 prompts, with one response per prompt, a 4,096-token context limit, and one policy update using a global reward baseline. LoGRA uses rank-256 RowAdam with mismatch subtraction and a predicted-KL budget annealed from 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} to 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} , whereas the dense baseline uses Adam with learning-rate annealing. We run three runs for 20,000 updates at 1.5B and 7B and 200 updates at 27B, retaining the 300-update annealing schedule for the latter. Figure 3: Training memory across model scales. Per-update peak allocated memory, averaged over three seeds, with ± \pm one sample standard deviation. Arrows compare temporal means over updates 1–200 at 1.5B/7B; at 27B, the arrow shows headroom to device capacity. Table 1: Accuracy, memory, and throughput of the main experiments. Memory and throughput cover full runs; accuracy peaks use updates 0–200. Peak memory is the maximum of the three-seed mean curve.

At 1.5B, LoGRA achieves peak Pass@1 of 67.87 % 67.87\% , compared with 63.77 % 63.77\% for Dense; peak Pass@4 increases from 80.33 % 80.33\% to 82.47 % 82.47\% . At 7B, the methods attain similar peak accuracy: 72.33 % 72.33\% versus 72.48 % 72.48\% Pass@1 and 85.13 % 85.13\% versus 85.33 % 85.33\% Pass@4 for LoGRA and Dense, respectively. LoGRA also trains the 27B model successfully, reaching 71.52 % 71.52\% Pass@1 and 81.87 % 81.87\% Pass@4, whereas Dense exhausts GPU memory at its first Adam-state allocation. These results show that compressed updates preserve competitive learning performance in the evaluated configurations while making the largest model trainable under the same GPU budget.

We presented LoGRA, a memory-efficient approach to LLM RL post-training that uses low-rank gradient sketches throughout gradient accumulation, weight updates, and policy synchronization. Our results show that compact gradient representations can substantially reduce training memory without sacrificing reasoning performance. In particular, LoGRA enables sustained training of a 27B model for over 1,100 steps on a single eight-GPU node, where dense Adam exceeds the available memory. Predicted-KL step control complements compression by regulating policy changes, with conservative budgets supporting stable long-horizon learning. Together, these findings highlight gradient representation as a practical lever for lowering the hardware barrier to RL post-training.

We evaluate LoGRA across multiple reasoning tasks with models ranging from 1.5B to 27B parameters. LoGRA reduces average training memory by 21.8% at 1.5B and 45.7% at 7B without sacrificing task performance. These savings also make larger-scale training feasible: LoGRA sustains stable learning of a 27B model for over 1,100 steps on a single eight-GPU node, where the dense Adam baseline runs out of memory under the same hardware allocation. Ablations further clarify how projection design and KL budgets affect learning performance and training stability.

Figure 3 shows that LoGRA lowers average per-update memory at 1.5B and 7B. Over the complete runs, average memory decreases from 9.18 to 7.18 GiB at 1.5B and from 31.82 to 17.29 GiB at 7B, reductions of 21.8% and 45.7%, respectively. Under the seed-averaged peak definition, LoGRA reduces peak memory from 9.19 to 8.66 GiB at 1.5B and from 31.85 to 22.26 GiB at 7B. At 27B, LoGRA uses 51.54 GiB on average and reaches a peak seed-averaged memory of 53.88 GiB; Dense fails before completing an update, precluding a measured memory-reduction ratio or throughput comparison. End-to-end update rates are similar where both methods complete training: 55.44 versus 54.28 updates/h at 1.5B and 25.73 versus 25.28 updates/h at 7B for LoGRA and Dense, respectively. The main systems benefit is reduced memory use and feasibility at 27B, with modest observed throughput gains at 1.5B and 7B.

inspect:2610.06621.question: For Frozen Factor or Spectral Band, what language-model fine-tuning task results compare frozen A, frozen B, spectral bands, and standard LoRA at matched rank, trainable-parameter budget, and training recipe? What limitations or counterexamples are reported?

passages.text: Spectral variants of low-rank adaptation (LoRA) choose both a subspace and which factor to freeze. We separate these choices by freezing the input factor A A or output factor B B on the top or bottom singular directions of pretrained weights, with learning rates selected separately. At rank 2, the same-band advantage of freezing A A is larger than either within-factor band difference on all four task–model pairs with complete comparisons. Freezing B B also trails comparable-budget free LoRA by 8–18 percentage points on five pairs spanning a formatting task and OpenBookQA. The A-frozen advantage persists in a single-GPU-model replication and within individual MLP module groups, including controls with equal or greater trainable counts for B frozen, and when A is frozen on a random orthonormal basis. The factor contrast weakens with rank. On OpenBookQA / Qwen2.5-1.5B at rank 16, PEFT’s MiCA implementation trails comparable-budget LoRA by 3.08 points under a shared training recipe transferred from the MiCA paper. A trained oracle output subspace largely removes the low-rank deficit; partial warm-up gains recur across three direction seeds. The factor-versus-band ordering is descriptive; an approximate multiplicity audit weakens several earlier significance claims. These results extend known factor asymmetry by showing how its magnitude depends on spectral placement, rank and training conditions.

LoRA adapts a pretrained weight matrix through a low-rank update B ​ A BA , where A A maps the layer input into a small intermediate representation and B B maps that representation to the output ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . Fixing one factor reduces the number of trainable parameters, but also fixes either the input or output subspace available to the update. A spectral construction makes another choice: which singular directions of the pretrained weight should define that subspace? Cross-method comparisons can entangle these choices. MiCA fixes the output factor on bottom singular directions ( Rüdiger and Raschka, 2026 ) ; PiCa’s implementation fixes an input-side projector on top directions and shares the trainable output factor across layers ( Hwang et al., 2026 ) . These correspond to freezing B B and A A , respectively (Appendix C.3 ). Comparing them changes orientation, band and sharing at once. Their within-method band ablations, by contrast, hold orientation fixed. The asymmetry between LoRA factors is already known. Zhu et al. (2024) show that training B B while fixing A A is often more effective than the reverse, including experiments with spectral factors. LoRA-FA fixes A A for memory efficiency ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , and LoRA+ improves training by assigning a larger learning rate to B B ( Hayou et al., 2024a ) . The question we address is narrower: how large is the frozen-factor contrast relative to the top-versus-bottom spectral contrast, and how does that comparison change with rank?

We use a two-by-two design: freeze A A or B B , each on the top or bottom band, while retaining the same pretrained model, data, adapted modules and training budget. Learning rates are selected separately for every configuration. We complement equal-rank comparisons with free LoRA at a nearby trainable-parameter count and a control that gives the B-frozen configuration more parameters than the A-frozen configuration. Figure 1 illustrates the main low-rank result. Figure 1: At rank 2, changing the frozen factor has a larger effect than switching spectral extremes. Points are mean test scores over five seeds at separately selected learning rates. The free-LoRA reference has rank 1 and a comparable, slightly larger trainable budget than rank-2 B-frozen LoRA. A-frozen LoRA has more trainable parameters at equal rank; Table 3 controls this advantage. The panels use different vertical scales. Lines connect configurations, not training trajectories. Full scores and uncertainty are in Tables 7 and 2 . At rank 2, the factor contrast exceeds the band contrast on all four complete comparisons. The A-frozen advantage survives parameter-count and module-group controls and does not require a spectral input basis on the two pairs tested. The factor contrast decreases along the complete OpenBookQA rank sweep, becoming comparable to the band contrast at rank 16. Finally, a subspace extracted from trained LoRA greatly improves B-frozen performance, showing that its low-rank deficit depends on placement.

Our contribution is to separate these design choices under optimization and budget controls and identify the limits of the resulting comparison. Factor asymmetry itself is not new. A follow-up evaluates PEFT’s MiCA implementation under a transferred recipe, without reproducing its original knowledge-acquisition benchmark or evaluating PiCa.

passages.text: Across the four complete rank-2 comparisons, freezing A A rather than B B improves mean performance by 6.6–19.0 percentage points on the same band. By comparison, switching between the top and bottom bands changes the score by at most 5.2 points within either orientation. This ordering holds within each of the four pairs; it is not an artifact of averaging positive and negative band effects. The corresponding averaged contrasts are shown in Table 2 and Figure 2 . passages.text: Against comparable-budget free LoRA, the top- and bottom-band B-frozen configurations lose 8–18 points on the five central pairs (Table 7 ). On OpenBookQA with Qwen2.5-1.5B, the bottom-band B-frozen score is 42.20%, equal to the unadapted model’s score, while free LoRA reaches 54.56%. On the formatting task, the base model never produces a fully valid output, so the gap measures how well each adapter learns the transformation. ARC-Challenge is a useful boundary case: at rank 2, the corresponding B-frozen deficits are only 2.0 and 3.8 points, alongside a smaller gain from fine-tuning itself.

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a standard approach for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, yet a fundamental practical question remains unresolved: how should the adapter rank be chosen? An overly small rank may lead to a poorly conditioned optimization landscape, whereas an unnecessarily large rank sacrifices the efficiency that motivates LoRA in the first place. Existing theoretical analyses provide only limited guidance on this trade-off, and their guarantees are typically established under restrictive theoretical settings. We address this gap by developing a substantially sharper landscape theory for LoRA, building on modern results from nonconvex low-rank matrix sensing. Our central insight is that the appropriate adapter rank should depend on the quality of the data-induced optimization geometry, rather than on the model alone. To formalize this connection, we introduce LoRA-RIP, a data-dependent restricted-isometry metric that characterizes the conditioning of the cross-entropy (CE) objective along LoRA-relevant low-rank directions. We prove that sufficient rank over-parameterization, with the required rank explicitly determined by the LoRA-RIP constant, eliminates spurious local minima, thereby extending existing RIP-based guarantees beyond the classical 1 / 3 1/3 regime. This characterization further enables principled data selection under a fixed rank budget. Experiments across language and vision tasks support these theoretical predictions, showing that rank and data quality are two coupled resources that should be jointly considered for more efficient and reliable LoRA fine-tuning.

• We develop a theoretical framework linking adapter rank r r and a newly introduced notion LoRA-RIP δ k LoRA \delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}} to global optimality in the balanced LoRA landscape. We show that as long as r / r ⋆ > ( 2 ​ δ k LoRA / ( 1 − δ k LoRA ) ) 2 r/r_{\star}>\left(2\delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}}/(1-\delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}})\right)^{2} , no spurious local minima exist in the landscape of Eq. ( 2 ), where r ⋆ r_{\star} denotes the rank of the global solution M ∗ M^{*} in Assumption 3.1 . This result establishes a sufficient rank threshold for a benign landscape. Our experiments further illustrate rank-dependent optimization trends consistent with this characterization. • We identify theoretically motivated data-selection principles such as latent-space coverage and pre-tuning softmax saturation. Our analysis links data composition to LoRA-RIP and shows how more favorable data geometry reduces the amount of rank-over-parameterization needed for a benign landscape. This yields a landscape-guided view of data selection in which data quality and adapter rank act as complementary resources.

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) has become a central parameter-efficient fine-tuning method, and numerous variants have been built on its structure, including quantized adapters ( Dettmers et al., 2023 ) , adaptive rank allocation ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , and modified factor updates ( Hayou et al., 2024 ) . Other work studies geometric updates and stabilization mechanisms ( Zhang and Pilanci, 2024 ; Yen et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) . Recent theory has studied LoRA from complementary angles. Expressivity results characterize what a given adapter rank can represent ( Zeng and Lee, 2024 ) . From the view of optimization, NTK-regime analysis gives benign landscape guarantees for a linearized fine-tuning model ( Jang et al., 2024 ) . Other works analyze nonlinear LoRA landscapes or gradient-flow dynamics under structural assumptions ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) .

We consider one language task and one vision task. For NLP, we fine-tune MPNet-base ( Song et al., 2020 ) on MNLI ( Williams et al., 2018 ) , a natural-language inference task in GLUE ( Wang et al., 2018 ) . For vision, we fine-tune a ViT-B/16 model ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2020 ) on CIFAR-100 ( Krizhevsky and Hinton, 2009 ) . In each run, we apply LoRA to the query projection in layer/block 10. Each experiment controls all other training choices except for the single factor being tested. Full protocols and complete results for the main-text experiments are provided in Appendix D . We further offer curvature diagnostics, multi-seed evaluations, and robustness studies across datasets and adaptation settings in Appendix E .

passages.section: Appendix E Landscape Diagnostics and Robustness Evaluations
passages.text: This section examines the optimization geometry and stability of LoRA fine-tuning through rank/checkpoint curvature, ambient matrix-space references, and multi-seed training. We also study the effects of data composition at a common reference point and along training trajectories, evaluate coverage across datasets, backbones, and adapter locations, and examine confidence-band selection on MNLI. The rank-sweep and MNLI data-intervention protocols are described in Appendix D . Together, these evaluations connect rank-dependent optimization gains to data-induced geometry and the practical effectiveness of landscape-guided selection.

Our theoretical analysis focuses on single-matrix LoRA fine-tuning with cross-entropy loss under low-rank target and LoRA-RIP assumptions. The resulting rank bounds are sufficient rather than necessary, leaving room for tighter characterizations of the relationship between adapter rank and data-induced geometry. Our empirical evaluation examines this relationship through controlled classification experiments across datasets and backbones. Extending the theory to joint multi-layer adaptation and evaluating the data-selection principles in larger-scale generative fine-tuning are natural directions for future work.

passages.text: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) offers many parameterizations, yet their methodological and functional differences remain unclear. We compare six methods in language and diffusion models to examine how their parameterizations relate to task performance, forgetting, and changes in pretrained weight geometry. Motivated by the spectrum-preserving design of orthogonal fine-tuning (OFT), we first ask whether spectral preservation is itself important for adaptation and retention. We find that the selected LoRA-family methods also approximately preserve pretrained geometry, and that restoring their slightly drifted singular-value spectra largely preserves task performance, questioning the necessity of explicit geometric preservation. Beyond this, we observe that some methods exhibit distinct adaptation–retention trade-offs that vary across settings: LoRA most consistently limits forgetting at competitive performance, DoRA achieves higher mean task scores than LoRA in most comparisons, while PiSSA often incurs greater retention costs. Further intervention experiments suggest that while performance gains from different PEFT methods can be attributed to modifications in different groups of spectral components, we consistently find that restoring dominant rather than intermediate or trailing components produces the largest mean reduction in general-text NLL or base-image drift. Together, these results motivate evaluating geometric constraints through their functional consequences rather than preservation alone. Code is available at https://github.com/Kuaaannn/PEFT_methods .

We address these questions by combining controlled empirical comparisons with direct interventions on pretrained weight geometry. We also review experimental controls in published PEFT comparisons to guide our study design ( Section 2 ). We study six representative methods, including LoRA, DoRA, PiSSA, MiLoRA, OFT, and HRA, across language-model adaptation and diffusion personalization. Rather than comparing parameterizations only through final task scores, we examine three levels of behavior: their operating performance after method-specific tuning, their retention of pretrained capabilities, and the functional consequences of the geometric changes they induce. As summarized in Figure 1 , this analysis reveals a recurring mismatch: parameterization labels can overstate geometric differences, whereas task scores can understate functional differences. Our study leads to three main findings. Explicit geometric preservation is not what primarily separates PEFT methods. We first characterize adaptation relative to the two-sided orthogonal orbit of the pretrained weights. For small isotropically oriented additive updates, the fraction of weight displacement appearing as singular-value displacement scales as 1 / max ⁡ ( m , n ) 1/\sqrt{\max(m,n)} , showing that limited spectral drift can arise even without an explicit orthogonality constraint. Consistent with this prediction, the LoRA-family methods we study exhibit only modest spectral drift and very small changes in hyperspherical energy. More importantly, restoring pretrained singular values while retaining the adapted singular bases largely preserves task performance. Thus, explicit geometric preservation is neither unique to successful PEFT nor, in our tested settings, necessary for retaining its task gains.

Similar task performance can conceal more persistent differences in retention. After method-specific learning-rate tuning, the six methods often achieve competitive downstream performance, but their retention behavior differs more systematically. Across the tested settings, LoRA most consistently limits forgetting while maintaining competitive performance. DoRA achieves higher mean task scores than LoRA in most comparisons, typically with some additional forgetting, whereas PiSSA often incurs larger retention costs. Crucially, tighter preservation of pretrained geometry does not reliably predict better retention. The more persistent distinctions between methods therefore appear in their functional consequences, rather than simply in the geometric invariants imposed by their parameterizations. Adaptation is spectrally heterogeneous, whereas forgetting is spectrally structured. We next intervene on dominant, intermediate, and trailing spectral components, ordered by pretrained singular value. For task adaptation, there is no universal spectral location of useful change: PiSSA consistently concentrates task-relevant changes in the dominant components, whereas for the other methods the sufficient components vary with the model, capacity, and task. For forgetting, however, a markedly more consistent pattern emerges: restoring the dominant components produces the largest mean reduction in general-text NLL or base-image drift across all six methods and tested settings. This ordering persists even in cases where the dominant-component edit is smaller in norm than alternative edits. These results suggest that downstream adaptation can be realized through multiple spectral routes, while forgetting is more consistently coupled to changes in dominant pretrained components.

In our settings, LoRA-family methods approximately preserve the spectra and hyperspherical energy that OFT is designed to preserve exactly. Singular-value restoration largely retains task performance. Tighter preservation must be judged by its task and retention outcomes.

Across the tested settings, our comparison of selected PEFT methods finds no consistent performance–retention advantage from explicit geometric preservation. With method-specific learning-rate tuning, LoRA most consistently limits forgetting while maintaining competitive task performance. Restoring pretrained singular values largely preserves task performance, while restoring dominant components consistently yields the largest mean reduction in forgetting, although its effects on task performance vary. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating adaptation and retention jointly. In addition, shared learning rates and single-seed results can bias comparisons, underscoring the need for method-specific tuning and evaluation across multiple seeds. We hope this study supports more reliable evaluations, informs method selection, and guides PEFT designs that better balance adaptation with the retention of pretrained capabilities.

passages.section: D.2 Task performance and forgetting across spectral components
passages.text: The dominant, intermediate and trailing component groups are approximate thirds adjusted to nearby pretrained spectral gaps. Restore and keep operations replace complete rank-one contributions, using pretrained singular values as in Eq. 4 . The measured response includes these interactions between components. Restoring dominant components reduces general drift in every checkpoint and gives the largest mean reduction for each method. It gives the largest individual reduction in 17 of 18 checkpoints. MiLoRA seed zero has a slightly larger trailing-component response. Class-prompt drift also decreases in every checkpoint, with dominant restoration giving the largest reduction. Both drift measures therefore support the recurring dominant-component response. CLIP responses differ, with LoRA’s mean general-prompt alignment decreasing. OFT gains fidelity on average but loses fidelity in one checkpoint. Keeping only the adapted dominant components nearly preserves mean fidelity for LoRA, DoRA and PiSSA. LoRA and DoRA reduce general drift in every checkpoint, whereas PiSSA retains essentially all its drift. These responses show that similar retained task performance can accompany different retention outcomes. Fidelity losses vary across seeds, including a larger DoRA loss. We report DINO changes directly and use the 1 pp sufficiency rule only for language accuracy. OFT/HRA have greater trained drift than PiSSA in these selected settings. Figure 16: FLUX component-restoration responses. The top row restores the named component group, and the bottom row keeps only that adapted group. All changes use the same-run trained model. Lines show method means and faint points show individual checkpoints.

candidates.title: A Riemannian Geometry for Low-rank Adaptation
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is widely used as a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique for pre-trained deep neural networks, which approximates the weight update via full fine-tuning by a low-rank matrix $BA^\top$. This parameterization leads to the equivalence relation $(B, A) \sim (BG^{-1}, AG^\top)$ for any invertible matrix $G$ because $BA^\top = BG^{-1}(AG^\top)^\top$ and thus both pairs yield the same loss value. This relation induces a quotient manifold where matrices $(BG^{-1}, AG^\top)$ for all $G$ are identified, eliminating redundant directions along which the loss value remains unchanged. To respect the geometry of this manifold, the original search space is endowed with a Riemannian metric that is invariant under the equivalence relation. Such a metric induces preconditioning at each gradient step and ensures that each weight update via LoRA changes the loss value, leading to efficient optimization. In this paper, we propose a new Riemannian metric that is specifically tailored to LoRA to close the gap to full fine-tuning at the weight level. candidates.title: Scaling Repeated-Data Pretraining: Batch Size, Regularization, and GPU-Time Tradeoffs
candidates.abstract_excerpt: We study pretraining when compute is abundant but unique training data are finite, requiring repeated training on the same data. We first revisit infinite-compute pretraining (Kim et al. 2026) and show that its frontier depends critically on choices previously fixed or studied only in isolation. In particular, optimizing batch size together with epoch counts reveals a U-shaped relationship between validation loss and batch size, favoring smaller batches than typical pretraining, likely because small-batch gradient noise provides implicit regularization. We further find that training recipes, previously optimized under a single-pass assumption, can be tuned, e.g., repacking documents into new sequences every epoch, weight tying, and positive embedding weight decay. We then relax the infinite-compute assumption. In particular, smaller-than-typical batch sizes can require prohibitively long sequential training, motivating to treat GPUs and time as separate resources. candidates.title: A Fine-Grained Analysis of the LoRA Fine-Tuning Landscape with Implications for Data Selection
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a standard approach for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, yet a fundamental practical question remains unresolved: how should the adapter rank be chosen? An overly small rank may lead to a poorly conditioned optimization landscape, whereas an unnecessarily large rank sacrifices the efficiency that motivates LoRA in the first place. Existing theoretical analyses provide only limited guidance on this trade-off, and their guarantees are typically established under restrictive theoretical settings. We address this gap by developing a substantially sharper landscape theory for LoRA, building on modern results from nonconvex low-rank matrix sensing. Our central insight is that the appropriate adapter rank should depend on the quality of the data-induced optimization geometry, rather than on the model alone. To formalize this connection, we introduce LoRA-RIP, a data-dependent restricted-isometry metric that characterizes the conditioning of the cross-entropy (CE) objective along LoRA-relevant low-rank directions. candidates.title: LoGRA: Scaling LLM Reinforcement Learning with Low-Rank Gradient Sketches
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Reinforcement learning has greatly advanced the capabilities of large language models, but its memory demands remain a barrier to broader adoption. We introduce LoGRA, an approach to RL post-training that reduces memory by retaining useful learning signals in low-rank gradient sketches. These compact representations support both model updates and efficient policy synchronization. To prevent overly large updates from disrupting learning, we complement gradient compression with predicted-KL step control, which estimates policy changes before applying each update and adjusts its magnitude accordingly. With all techniques combined, LoGRA reduces average training memory usage by up to 45.7% across reasoning tasks without compromising performance. It also enables stable training of a 27B-parameter model for over 1,100 steps on a single eight-GPU node, where dense Adam runs out of memory, making previously memory-infeasible RL training practical. Code is available in the \href{https://github.com/skzhang1/labs-molt/tree/logra/examples/scripts/logra}{Molt library}.

candidates.title: Adaptive Utilization of Low-Rank Adaptation via Conditioned Gating
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) achieves parameter-efficient fine-tuning by constraining model updates to a low-rank subspace and has been widely used in practice. candidates.title: ORCA: The Annealed Spectral Conditioning Optimizer for Faster, Better LLM Training
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Modern LLM optimizers such as Muon often produce weight matrices with higher effective rank than Adam, yet further spectral control has delivered only modest gains. We identify a tension behind this result: concentrated spectra can suppress gradient directions in coupled weight matrices and slow optimization, while constraints maintained throughout training can limit task-specific adaptation and raise the attainable loss floor. We introduce ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After), a minimal optimizer intervention that applies strong but temporary soft orthogonality regularization early in training, then removes it. This allows the weights to benefit from a broader spectrum early on and adapt freely afterward. Across LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained mixture-of-experts models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon. Its loss reduction relative to Muon matches or exceeds Muon's reduction relative to Adam. Ablations support the early-shaping, later-release design. Further, ORCA requires no architectural changes and adds minimal overhead. An implementation is available at https://github.com/uuurraaa/ORCA_Optimizer.

candidates.title: Where to Adapt Matters: Layer-Selective Fine-Tuning for Capability Retention
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) enables large language models (LLMs) to adapt to specialized tasks, but often at the cost of degrading general capabilities acquired during pretraining. candidates.title: Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional $\ell_2$ weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with $124$M to $500$M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. Under fixed-horizon training with $60\%$ label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched $\ell_2$ regularization by up to $17.8$ points on MNIST and $4.6$ points across four BERT-base tasks. candidates.title: PGSB: Pretrained-Guided Shared Basis for LoRA Model Merging
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Large pretrained models have achieved remarkable success across diverse domains, yet adapting them to multiple downstream tasks remains challenging: full fine-tuning is costly, while maintaining separate task-specific models is storage-inefficient and fails to produce a unified multi-task model. candidates.abstract_excerpt: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) offers many parameterizations, yet their methodological and functional differences remain unclear. candidates.abstract_excerpt: On-device learning is necessary when the model encounters user-,sensor-, or environment-specific shifts after deployment. candidates.title: Activation Denoising: A Robustness View on Parallel vs Sequential LLM Quantization
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Post-training quantization is a powerful tool for compressing large language models. The most scalable methods quantize every layer in parallel, but quantization errors then compound through the residual stream, as no layer corrects for the errors of the layers before it. candidates.title: Shared Low-rank Basis Factorization for Data-free Mixture-of-Experts Compression
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models decouple capacity from compute through sparse routing, but their large parameter count creates storage and serving challenges. candidates.title: D-SLR: The Disjoint Row-Sparse plus Low-Rank Decomposition
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Compressing a matrix for reconstruction still defaults to the truncated SVD, approximating the data with a single low-rank structure. candidates.abstract_excerpt: Muon has motivated a growing family of optimizers that compose multiple matrix normalizations, but these methods remain fragmented and lack a unified perspective. We introduce chained linear minimization oracles (chained LMOs), which cast these methods as compositions of LMOs. Despite their empirical success, many chains fall outside the standard LMO framework and can diverge on smooth convex objectives. To explain why composition can nevertheless help, we turn to linear associative memory and show that chaining can improve over Muon under anisotropic embeddings. Empirically, we propose TensorChain, a novel optimizer within the framework that stacks compatible weight matrices across different layers and normalizes the 3d tensor across its axes. In Qwen3 0.6B and 1.7B pretraining, TensorChain outperforms all chained baselines in average token efficiency, with average token savings of 9.6% over Muon at matched validation loss.

candidates.title: When Rank Rises as LLMs Degrade
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Post-training adapts language models in non-stationary environments. Practitioners monitor representation health with RankMe and related spectral statistics, often assuming that rank falls when representations degrade. We show that this assumption is unsafe for LLM post-training. In a controlled study of Qwen3-0.6B with four degradation modes and three seeds, data duplication worsens held-out loss by 75% relative to healthy while increasing both original and centred RankMe; the latter changes by 13.5 pooled standard deviations. Covariance effective rank rises to nearly twice its healthy value. This failure is spectral dispersion rather than collapse, so a one-sided monitor rates the worst checkpoint as the healthiest. By contrast, a learning-rate misconfiguration lowers centred RankMe and k95, while uncentred RankMe is inconsistent across seeds. Direction is therefore a property of the regime-statistic pair and cannot be fixed by recalibration alone. We also distinguish two often-conflated statistics: RankMe normalises singular values, whereas covariance effective rank normalises eigenvalues. candidates.title: How Learning Governs Unlearning across the Memorization-Generalization Spectrum
candidates.abstract_excerpt: While unlearning seeks to negate undesired capabilities acquired through learning, little research has examined how the way models learn shapes their subsequent unlearning. In this paper, we investigate this connection from the perspectives of memorization and generalization, the two most representative yet competing strategies that models employ during training. We first classify memorization- and generalization-heavy models using grokking in modular addition and compare their responses to unlearning, showing that the latter suffer greater retain damage, i.e., a larger performance drop on the retain set. Furthermore, we conduct a finer-grained analysis by introducing bucketed modular addition, in which the respective contributions of the two strategies can be explicitly controlled across the memorization-generalization spectrum. In this setup, we reaffirm that the same trend persists and is nearly monotonic. We further demonstrate that this relationship also holds in LLM unlearning across verbatim and factual recall settings. candidates.title: A Solvable Model of Adaptive Learning Rate Rescaling: Acceleration, Stability & Scaling
candidates.abstract_excerpt: A recurring design principle in modern optimizers is to decouple update magnitude from the raw gradient norm, yet its consequences for learning-curve and resource scaling remain unclear. We isolate this mechanism by studying normalized SGD in a random-feature model with power-law teacher and data covariance. Fixed-norm updates induce an effective learning rate that grows as gradients shrink. We derive a dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) describing the joint dependence of the loss on training time, model width and batch size. Normalization initially accelerates SGD, mapping the power-law exponent $r_{\rm SGD}<1$ to $2r_{\rm SGD}/(1-r_{\rm SGD})$, with exponential convergence at $r_{\rm SGD}=1$ and formal finite-time convergence for $r_{\rm SGD}>1$. At finite step size, however, the same feedback ultimately breaks the acceleration and leads to marginal stability. The late-time theory yields width-limited, edge-of-stochastic-stability (EoSS), and deterministic edge-of-stability (EoS) regimes. candidates.title: Lightweight and Versatile Learned Optimization by Recombination of Gradient History
candidates.abstract_excerpt: This paper presents a lightweight and versatile learned optimizer that dynamically recombines gradient history, represented as averages over disjoint time spans. The optimizer reduces the prediction space to one scalar coefficient per gradient average, shared by multiple parameters. Progressively averaging older gradients minimizes memory cost of long history, while keeping their contributions independently accessible. A 37k-parameter network trained in 0.87 GPU-hours generalizes zero-shot to unseen tasks, lowering validation loss by 9.1% and 0.4% on BERT-Tiny and GPT-Tiny, and improving test accuracy over Adam by 3.5 %p on a Vision Transformer and by 2.7 %p on average across nine graph models, with FLOPs overhead as low as 0.3%.

candidates.title: Training-Free Transformer Merging via Sequential Local Operator Alignment
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Training-free model merging aims to combine multiple fine-tuned models into a single model without further optimization on labeled data. Yet, in transformers, independently merging individual layers can affect a shared attention computation because the query-key and value-output operators depend on composed matrices, overlooking the functional structure. Moreover, when merging earlier components, downstream components receive different activations than they do in the original model, thus, the merged and original execution paths no longer match. In this paper, we introduce Sequential Local Operator Alignment, a training-free method that merges transformers along the execution path of the partially merged model. Our method uses calibration data to estimate the local behavior of each functional component, aligns operators sequentially under the intermediate activation of the partially merged model, and subsequently factorizes the merged operators back into valid transformer parameters. We empirically show that this sequential step reduces error accumulation across layers. candidates.title: Layer-wise Input Recoverability in Deep Neural Networks
candidates.abstract_excerpt: The inner workings of deep neural networks are still not well understood. The information bottleneck framework, which characterizes deep networks by the mutual information between their hidden representations and the network's input, has been used to identify compression of input information with respect to an input image and output labels. We instead study how much of a layer's own input is recoverable from the layer's output in convolutional neural networks (CNNs). A convolutional layer applies its filters to one input patch at a time, so we evaluate recoverability on sampled input patches with a reconstruction-based probe and not on the entire feature map. The probe's size thus depends on channels and kernel size and not on feature map size, which lets our method scale to deep CNNs with wide feature maps. For each layer, we compare pretrained, random, and reconstruction-optimized encoders, using linear and linear-plus-residual-MLP decoders. We measure recoverability as $R^2$ between input patches and their reconstructions on a held-out set. Across nine ImageNet CNNs, recoverability generally decreases with depth but is more consistently predicted by the compression of the layer.

passages.text: However, we argue that this trade-off is not fundamental. Spectral regularization may be most valuable early, when it can shape the optimization trajectory, yet become a liability if maintained as the weights adapt to the task. The two effects need not be accepted together: we can use the constraint to shape the spectrum, then release it before it restricts the final solution. This motivates a minimal method ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After): During an initial phase, ORCA applies a soft orthogonality penalty, R orth ​ ( 𝐖 ) = 1 4 ​ ‖ 𝐖𝐖 ⊤ − 𝐈 ‖ F 2 R_{\mathrm{orth}}(\mathbf{W})=\frac{1}{4}\|\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\top}-\mathbf{I}\|_{F}^{2} . Then directly removes it at a single switch point. Training thereafter follows the standard optimizer update, with no gradual decay or further changes. This design lets early regularization influence the optimization path without prescribing the spectrum throughout training. In our experiments, this simple release is followed by faster loss reduction and a lower final validation loss than Muon. Figure 1.1: LLaMA 130M training dynamics. Effective rank is measured on a middle-layer V V projection; the dashed line marks regularization release. Figure 1.1 illustrates the transition. While the penalty is active, the effective rank of the weight matrix rises sharply above Muon’s, although ORCA initially has a higher validation loss. After release, the rank falls from its peak but remains above Muon’s, while validation loss decreases rapidly, crosses the Muon curve. The result is consistent with early spectral shaping leaving a useful effect on the subsequent trajectory, even after the explicit penalty is gone. Controlled interventions in Section 5 further investigates into this connection.

We evaluate ORCA on LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained MoE models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, including 100B-token training runs. ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon across these settings. In most experiments, the reduction is 0.02–0.04, comparable to or greater than Muon’s gain over Adam. To put this loss reduction in perspective, on LLaMA 1.3B, ORCA achieving the 0.024 lower validation loss reaches Muon’s 100k-step loss in just 60k steps. Further, downstream evaluations, alternative early spectral interventions, multi-seed runs, and ablations of method parameters and intervention timing further support these gains. Together, these results show that early spectral shaping followed by constraint relaxation can improve training efficiency and final performance across architectures without substantial changes to the optimizer. To summarize the contributions of the paper: (1) We illustrate a trade-off in spectral control through a simplified model and empirical observations: favorable spectra can accelerate optimization but persistent constraints may harm the attainable solution quality. (2) We introduce ORCA, a minimal shape-then-release optimizer that leverages early orthogonal regularization to improve optimization trajectories while allowing unconstrained adaptation in later training. (3) We demonstrate ORCA’s effectiveness across diverse LLM architectures and scales, achieving faster convergence and lower loss than existing optimizers. Through extensive controlled experiments, we further validate the mechanism that early effective-rank shaping drives the observed improvements.

The advantage of ORCA holds over a wide range of learning rates: at every learning rate evaluated for both methods, ORCA reaches a lower final validation loss than Muon, and at all evaluated configurations between 10 − 3 10^{-3} and 5 × 10 − 3 5\times 10^{-3} it is even better than fully tuned Muon. LLama Pretraining Tasks. We compare ORCA against Adam and Muon on LLaMA 350M and 1.3B, training each model for 100B tokens. As shown in Figure 4.1 , Muon outperforms Adam at both scales, while ORCA further lowers the validation loss. Compared with Muon, ORCA reduces the final loss by 0.0194 0.0194 at 350M and 0.0244 0.0244 at 1.3B, with consistent gains at both scales. Further, a four-seed robustness result for the 130M, 50k-step setting is reported in Appendix C . We also evaluate the final ORCA and Muon LLaMA 1.3B checkpoints from Figure 4.1 on five downstream tasks ( Clark et al., 2018 ; Zellers et al., 2019 ; Sakaguchi et al., 2021 ; Bisk et al., 2020 ) . As shown in Table 4.1 , ORCA outperforms Muon on all five tasks. This suggests that the lower pre-training loss of ORCA also leads to better downstream performance.

We also evaluate how the optimization performance translates into token efficiency by measuring the training required to reach a common target loss. We continued ORCA from its original 51k-step checkpoint, starting the final decay early, and reached a validation loss of 2.318 at approximately 60k steps. Therefore, ORCA used 40% fewer tokens to reach this target, a 1.66× token-efficiency gain. To save compute, we reused the checkpoint without retuning ORCA for the shorter run: its original 25k-step shaping stage accounts for 41.7% of the 60k-step budget rather than the tuned default of 25%. Further, downstream evaluations, alternative early spectral interventions, multi-seed runs, and ablations of method parameters and intervention timing further support these gains. Together, these results show that early spectral shaping followed by constraint relaxation can improve training efficiency and final performance across architectures without substantial changes to the optimizer. To summarize the contributions of the paper: (1) We illustrate a trade-off in spectral control through a simplified model and empirical observations: favorable spectra can accelerate optimization but persistent constraints may harm the attainable solution quality. (2) We introduce ORCA, a minimal shape-then-release optimizer that leverages early orthogonal regularization to improve optimization trajectories while allowing unconstrained adaptation in later training. (3) We demonstrate ORCA’s effectiveness across diverse LLM architectures and scales, achieving faster convergence and lower loss than existing optimizers. Through extensive controlled experiments, we further validate the mechanism that early effective-rank shaping drives the observed improvements.

The advantage of ORCA holds over a wide range of learning rates: at every learning rate evaluated for both methods, ORCA reaches a lower final validation loss than Muon, and at all evaluated configurations between 10 − 3 10^{-3} and 5 × 10 − 3 5\times 10^{-3} it is even better than fully tuned Muon. The independent searches select 1.3 × 10 − 3 1.3\times 10^{-3} , 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} , 10 − 3 10^{-3} , and 2 × 10 − 3 2\times 10^{-3} for Adam, Muon, Pion, and ORCA, with final validation losses of 2.8824 2.8824 , 2.8460 2.8460 , 2.9790 2.9790 , and 2.8106 2.8106 , respectively; ORCA thus lowers the loss by a further 0.0354 0.0354 relative to the best Muon and stays within 0.002 0.002 of its own optimum across 1.6 × 10 − 3 1.6\times 10^{-3} to 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} , showing that the improvement does not rely on a narrow learning-rate choice. LLama Pretraining Tasks. We compare ORCA against Adam and Muon on LLaMA 350M and 1.3B, training each model for 100B tokens. As shown in Figure 4.1 , Muon outperforms Adam at both scales, while ORCA further lowers the validation loss. Compared with Muon, ORCA reduces the final loss by 0.0194 0.0194 at 350M and 0.0244 0.0244 at 1.3B, with consistent gains at both scales. Further, a four-seed robustness result for the 130M, 50k-step setting is reported in Appendix C . We also evaluate the final ORCA and Muon LLaMA 1.3B checkpoints from Figure 4.1 on five downstream tasks ( Clark et al., 2018 ; Zellers et al., 2019 ; Sakaguchi et al., 2021 ; Bisk et al., 2020 ) . As shown in Table 4.1 , ORCA outperforms Muon on all five tasks. This suggests that the lower pre-training loss of ORCA also leads to better downstream performance.
